candidates.taskText: I run a 14-person structural engineering firm that's been subcontracting to two general contractors for eight years. One of them just offered to buy 40% of our firm for $600,000, which would give them priority on our capacity and a board seat. The other option: a regional infrastructure fund wants to lend us $500,000 at 7% to open a second office in a neighboring state, no equity given up, but we'd carry the debt regardless of how the expansion performs. Both offers expire at the end of the month because both parties are finalizing their own year-end plans. Taking the equity deal locks us into that contractor's project pipeline, which is currently strong but has been cyclical before. Taking the loan keeps us independent but doubles our overhead risk if the new office underperforms. We can't do both; the equity partner's term sheet explicitly forbids us from taking on this kind of debt. Which path should we commit to?

My co-founder and I have run a subscription meal-kit business for three years, currently at $2.1M annual revenue with thin margins. A larger food-delivery platform wants to acquire us outright for $3.4M, folding our brand into their app within six months. Separately, a group of our own investors is willing to put in $1.2M more to let us build our own delivery fleet and go direct-to-consumer in two additional cities, but that means at least two more years before we see profit, and the investors want a decision this quarter before they commit that capital elsewhere. Selling ends the business as an independent entity but gives us certainty and cash now. Expanding keeps us in control but the market for meal kits has been flattening nationally, and we don't have hard data on demand in the two target cities. Both paths close off the other once chosen. Which direction should we take?

We've already decided to consolidate our three regional call centers into one facility over the next five months — that decision is final and the lease on the new site is signed. The new site has room for 220 workstations, but we currently employ 260 agents across the three old sites, and attrition has been running at about 4% a month, which would naturally get us close to the new headcount by month four if we don't backfill departures at the old sites. Two of the old leases end in 60 days, one doesn't end for 150 days. We also need to migrate phone systems and retrain agents on a new ticketing platform, which vendor says takes 3 weeks per batch of 50 people and they can only run one batch at a time. Customer call volume is seasonal and peaks in month three of the transition, which is also when the two shorter leases expire. Given these constraints, how should we sequence the site closures, hiring freeze, and platform migration so we don't create a coverage gap during peak volume?

Our winery has committed to tripling case production this year to meet a new distribution contract with a national retailer — the contract is signed and the volume is fixed at 45,000 cases, up from 15,000 last year. We have one bottling line that runs at 800 cases per day, and it needs a 2-day changeover between different SKUs. The contract requires four different SKUs delivered in staggered shipments starting in month two and continuing monthly through month nine. Our current cellar can hold fermented wine for at most 60 days before it needs to move to bottling or start degrading, and we have three fermentation tanks total, each taking 21 days per batch. Labor for bottling is currently two shifts of 6 people; we can add a third shift but our labor contractor needs 3 weeks notice to supply extra staff. Given these fixed constraints, how should we schedule fermentation batches, bottling runs, and shipments to hit the contract's monthly delivery dates without gaps or spoilage?

I own a family-run Italian deli that's been in the same neighborhood for 52 years. Our longtime customers, mostly older residents, love that we still use handwritten chalkboard menus and paper butcher-wrap, and several have told us it's why they trust the quality. But the neighborhood has changed a lot in the last decade — younger renters and professionals now make up most of the foot traffic, and several have mentioned on our social media that the shop 'feels like walking into a time capsule' in a way that reads as a compliment online but seems to translate into them not coming in as regular customers, just occasional novelty visitors. We're not changing the recipes or the physical shop, and we're not planning to move upmarket or add anything trendy like avocado toast. But we do need to figure out how the deli presents itself — in signage, packaging, and how we talk about ourselves publicly — so that it draws in the newer residents as regulars without alienating the older ones who've been loyal for decades. How should we think about the identity and voice of this place going forward?

I co-founded a boutique fitness studio three years ago under the name 'Iron Bloom,' targeting women who wanted a tougher, less pastel alternative to typical women's fitness branding. It worked well locally — we built a loyal base of about 400 members — but as we prepare to open two more locations in different cities, our marketing consultant pointed out that 'Iron Bloom' tests ambiguously with people who've never heard of us: some assume it's a florist, others assume it's a men's gym. We're not changing our class formats, pricing, or trainer model — those are staying exactly as they are. The question is entirely about how the studio should present itself as we scale: whether to keep the name and invest in explaining it, adjust the name while preserving the tone we've built, or rethink the visual identity and voice more broadly so it reads clearly to new audiences in cities where we have zero existing reputation. What direction should we take with the name and creative identity as we expand?

Our mid-sized hospital started a new nurse-mentorship program eight months ago, pairing new hires with senior staff for the first 90 days. Since then, first-year nurse turnover dropped from 22% to 14%. However, in that same period we also raised starting nurse pay by 6% to stay competitive with a hospital across town, and we tightened hiring criteria to require at least one year of clinical rotation experience during nursing school, which we didn't require before. All three changes rolled out within about six weeks of each other, so the timelines overlap heavily. HR wants to expand the mentorship program hospital-wide next year, arguing it's clearly working, but finance is skeptical since the pay raise alone could plausibly explain a lot of the retention improvement, and stricter hiring criteria could mean we're simply retaining people who were always going to stay longer regardless of mentorship. We have turnover numbers broken down by unit and hire date, and mentorship coverage wasn't uniform — about 65% of new hires got a mentor, the rest didn't due to staffing gaps, though the two groups aren't documented as randomly assigned. What does this data actually tell us about whether the mentorship program is responsible for the retention improvement?

Our city's public library system tested a new late-fee elimination policy in six branches last year while the other nine branches kept the old fee structure. Circulation at the fee-free branches rose 19% over the year, and the library board is treating that as strong evidence the policy drives engagement. But looking closer, the six fee-free branches were chosen because they had the newest buildings, having just undergone renovations with more computers, longer hours, and updated children's sections in the two years prior, while the nine comparison branches are older with reduced staff hours due to budget cuts during the same period. We also changed our card registration process system-wide halfway through the year, which affected all fifteen branches equally, so that shouldn't explain the gap. I have month-by-month circulation numbers for all fifteen branches going back three years. Given these confounds, what does the circulation data actually tell us about whether eliminating late fees increased engagement?

I run a mid-sized accounting firm that mostly serves small businesses with annual tax filing and basic bookkeeping. Several of our long-term clients have started asking whether we can also help with ongoing cash-flow forecasting and light CFO-style advisory work throughout the year, not just at tax time. We have three senior accountants who have the skill for this kind of advisory work but are already at capacity during tax season, and slower the rest of the year. We're not deciding whether to offer something new in principle — we've agreed we want to build an advisory offering — but we haven't figured out what it should actually include, how it should be tiered for different client sizes, or how the ongoing relationship should be structured versus our current one-time annual engagement model. What should this advisory service look like in terms of scope and structure?

My company runs a chain of independent movie theaters, and we've committed to launching a loyalty membership program next quarter — that decision is final and we've already budgeted $80,000 for the first year of the program, mostly for the software platform and initial marketing. What we haven't settled is what the membership should actually offer members. We know from comps that most theater loyalty programs offer either point accumulation toward free tickets, flat monthly subscriptions for a set number of films, or tiered access with perks like reserved seating and discounted concessions. We serve a mix of casual moviegoers who come once every couple months and a smaller group of regulars who come weekly, and we don't want to design something so generous it caters only to the small heavy-user group while ignoring the larger casual base, or so thin that it doesn't feel worth signing up for. What should the actual membership structure and benefits look like?

Our nonprofit just received a one-time $250,000 bequest from a longtime donor's estate, with no restrictions on how it's used. We have three pressing claims on it: our after-school tutoring program needs $90,000 to cover a funding cliff next year when a grant expires, our building has a roof that inspectors say needs $110,000 in repairs within the next 18 months or risk water damage to program space, and our board has been wanting to build a modest reserve fund, currently at zero, to avoid the cash-flow crunches we hit every summer when donations dip. We can't fully fund all three with $250,000. The tutoring program serves 140 kids currently and would have to shut down without bridge funding. The roof repair is not urgent this month but becomes urgent within the timeframe given. The reserve fund has no deadline but the board has flagged it as a recurring vulnerability for three years running. How should we divide this money across these three needs?

I manage the equipment budget for a mid-sized manufacturing plant, and we have $180,000 approved for capital equipment this fiscal year, which must be spent or the unused portion reverts to corporate at year-end. Three department heads have submitted requests: the machining floor wants a $95,000 CNC upgrade that would cut cycle time by roughly 15% based on the vendor's estimate, the packaging line wants $70,000 for a new sealing machine to replace one that's failed twice this year and is out of warranty, and quality control wants $60,000 for updated inspection sensors to reduce the defect rate that's currently costing us about $40,000 a year in returns. Combined these requests total $225,000, which is $45,000 over budget. All three departments have legitimate, documented need, and none of the equipment can be financed on a payment plan under our current corporate policy — it has to be paid in full this year or not at all. How should the $180,000 be allocated across these three requests?
